title: Fitting an oak saddle threshold
subtitle: Cut and fix a solid oak saddle threshold bar across a doorway to cover the expansion gap and give a clean transition between two floor finishes
excerpt: How to fit a solid oak saddle threshold at a doorway. Covers measuring the opening, cutting the threshold to length, drilling and countersinking fixing holes, fitting and securing the bar, and sanding the top face flush.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK trade joinery practice for floor transitions.

glossaryTerms.definition: A flat or slightly humped bar of solid timber, metal, or composite material fitted across a doorway opening at floor level. It covers the expansion gap between two floor surfaces, protects the edges of both floor finishes, and provides a clean visual transition. Oak is the most common hardwood choice for domestic use.

A gap left between the edge of a floating floor and any fixed structure such as a wall, door frame, or threshold. The gap allows the floor to expand and contract with changes in temperature and humidity without buckling. Typically 10 to 12 mm wide for engineered timber; covered by a skirting board or threshold bar.

content.text: An oak saddle threshold is a solid hardwood bar fitted across a doorway where two floor levels or floor materials meet. It covers the
and protects the flooring edges, giving a clean visual transition. BEGINNER: basic sawing and drilling; the hardest part is a clean cut to exact width.
Measure the door opening from doorstop to doorstop. A

typically sits between the two doorstops so the door can close over it. Mark the cut line with a combination square across both faces of the oak, ensuring the line is square to the length. Cut with a fine-tooth crosscut saw, holding the timber firmly. Sand any roughness from the cut end with the sanding block.

Lay the threshold in position and check that the door closes cleanly over it without binding. If the threshold is too thick for the door to clear, plane or sand the top face down gradually, testing after each pass. If the subfloor level differs on each side of the doorway, the threshold base may need to be undercut to sit flat across the step: scribe from the lower side and remove the material with a chisel.

Drill two or three countersunk clearance holes through the threshold at evenly spaced positions along its length, keeping holes at least 30 mm from each end. Position holes toward the centre of the threshold width so the fixings land in the subfloor below and not in the edge of a floating floor board. Use a plug cutter to pre-cut oak pellets from offcut material if you want to conceal the screw heads.

Apply a small bead of construction adhesive to the underside of the threshold to prevent any rocking or creaking. Press into position and drive screws through the countersunk holes into the subfloor. Glue and tap in oak pellets over the screw heads if used, cutting flush when dry. Sand the top face along the grain to give an even surface, working from coarse to fine abrasive.

attrs.symptom: Door binds or scrapes on the threshold when closing
attrs.cause: The threshold is too tall for the door clearance.
attrs.fix: Remove the threshold and plane or sand the top face down in small increments, testing the door clearance after each pass.

attrs.cause: The underside of the threshold spans an uneven floor and does not bear evenly across its length.
attrs.fix: Remove and scribe the underside to the floor level using a compass, plane to the scribe line, and re-fix.
